opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm not sure they top out anywhere we'd recognize as a hard ceiling, at least not anytime soon. People have been predicting the wall for years, and every time we've found another axis to push on. First it was scaling pretraining: more data, more compute, bigger models. Then, when people started worrying we were running out of high-quality data, reinforcement learning on top of these models opened up a whole new dimension. Letting the model think longer, try things, get feedback, and learn from that turned out to be enormously powerful.

So I'd separate two questions. One is whether the transformer as an architecture is the final word. Probably not. There will be improvements in efficiency, memory, and how we handle really long contexts. But the architecture has been remarkably robust, and most of the gains have come from what we train it on and how we train it, not from swapping out the core block.

The other question is whether the overall paradigm of large neural networks trained with lots of compute, then refined with RL, tops out. I don't see evidence of that. What I do see is that the bottlenecks keep shifting. Sometimes it's compute, sometimes it's data, sometimes it's figuring out the right environments and reward signals so models learn skills that actually generalize. Those are hard problems, but they're engineering and research problems, not fundamental limits.

If I had to bet, I'd say these models will get to the point where they do a large fraction of economically valuable intellectual work, including a lot of research itself. Whether that's "topping out" or just the start of something else, I think we'll find out sooner than most people expect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shifting bottlenecks and continued training, but does not say that a transformer left without further training becomes less useful as the world changes.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize transformers as tools whose effective use depends on human orchestration.

r003.rationale: It does not identify reliance on a lab to retrain the model as a fundamental limitation on acquiring new capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think they top out in the way most people mean when they ask that. The question usually assumes there's some ceiling baked into the architecture, that at some point you'll stack more layers and more data and the curve just goes flat. I've been looking for that wall for years now and I keep not finding it.

What I actually believe is that the transformer is not the interesting part. It's a very good general-purpose function approximator that happens to be extremely friendly to the hardware we have. The thing that determines where models top out is what you're asking them to learn and how you're giving them feedback. For a long time that was next-token prediction on internet text, and you can argue that has a ceiling, because the internet only contains so much reasoning that's actually written down. People don't write out the thought process that led to the answer, they just write the answer.

The reason I'm not worried about the architecture is that once you let the model think for a long time before it answers, and you train it on whether the final result was right, you've changed what the limit is. Now the limit isn't how much human reasoning exists on the web, it's how good your verifier is and how much compute you're willing to spend letting the model explore. That's a very different kind of ceiling, and it's one that moves every time you make the training signal better.

If you forced me to name a real constraint, I'd say it's the environments. Math and code are wonderful because you can check the answer. Most of the world isn't like that. Figuring out how to give a model honest feedback on a fuzzy, long-horizon task is harder than anything about attention mechanisms. So when people ask where transformers top out, my honest answer is that we'll probably replace pieces of the architecture before we ever hit its limit, and the thing we'll actually be stuck on is teaching the model to tell when it's wrong.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think we know yet. I’d be skeptical of anyone who says we’ve found the ceiling, but also of anyone who says there isn’t one. When a model stops improving, you have to ask: Is that a limitation of the architecture, the data, or the way we’re training it?

Transformers are one part of a much larger system. You can change how a model learns, give it more time to work through a problem, or let it interact with an environment and learn from feedback. Those might take us further without requiring a completely new architecture.

So I’d frame the question as: What’s the next bottleneck, and can we demonstrate a way around it? I don’t think we have enough evidence to put a firm upper bound on transformer-based models.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think we know yet. There’s a difference between asking where the transformer architecture tops out and asking where the current way of training these models tops out. You might hit diminishing returns on predicting the next token from internet text without having exhausted what the architecture can learn.

The question for me is whether a model can keep improving by trying things, getting feedback, and correcting its mistakes. Can it learn to solve problems that aren’t already represented in its training data? And can we give it more time to think and get reliably better answers?

If those things keep working, there may be a lot of room left. We’ll probably change pieces of the architecture along the way. But I wouldn’t confidently draw a line today and say, ‘Transformers can get this far, and no further.’
